title: Doubt
hookLine: doubt as a hindrance and as honest questioning
tomorrow: a flat, boring feeling: can it ever be pleasant?

lines: WHAT IF NONE OF THIS DOES ANYTHING?
WHICH ONE IS TELLING THE TRUTH?
cards: It's the question that turns up at one in the morning, or halfway through a chemistry lab: what if none of this actually does anything? Mai typed it, deleted it, and typed it again.
A question like that can seem disloyal, as if a real practitioner would never ask it. A town in the Buddha's time had the same trouble.

Teacher after teacher passed through Kesaputta, each praising his own view and tearing down the rest. So the people there, the Kalamas, brought the Buddha one honest question: which of these teachers is telling the truth?

teach.b: The Buddha's answer is easy to misquote. First he tells the Kalamas it's fitting for them to doubt, fitting to be uncertain, in a matter that really is uncertain.

teach.h: NOT BY REPORT, TRADITION OR CHARM.
teach.b: Then he says: don't go by reports, or tradition, or scripture, or clever reasoning, or a speaker's charm, or the thought that this monk is our teacher.

teach.h: KNOW FOR YOURSELVES: HARM OR WELFARE?
teach.b: When you know for yourselves that something is unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and leads to harm and suffering, let it go. When you know something leads to welfare and happiness, take it up. Notice what he didn't say.
Not believe whatever feels right. He gave them a test, and pointed it at greed, hatred and delusion and what they do to a life. So Buddhist teaching knows two kinds of doubt.

teach.h: WAVERING, OR A DOUBT THAT CHECKS.
teach.b: One is vicikiccha, listed among the hindrances: a wavering that never commits, that keeps you from trying anything long enough to find out.
The other is the honest questioning the Buddha welcomes here: a doubt that goes and checks. The difference isn't whether you have questions. It's what you do with them.
The Kalamas didn't walk off. They asked, and then they had something to test against their own lives.

how: Buddhist teachers often point to the Kalama Sutta when students raise doubts: questions are welcome, and teachings are tested against whether they lead to harm or to welfare, alongside what the wise praise.

o: a sign that you've lost your faith for good
uncertainty: either wavering, or honest checking
a sin that cuts a person off from the Buddha

games.q: the Kalamas' question — tap the pairs.
p: heard too many teachers, asked who was right
part of the test for letting go

s: the Kalama Sutta says believe whatever feels right to you
it gives a test: what leads to harm or to welfare, and what the wise blame or praise.
the Buddha told the Kalamas it was fitting to doubt
in a matter that's uncertain, he says, doubt is fitting.
in Buddhism, every doubt is a hindrance to push down
wavering that never tries is a hindrance; honest questioning that checks is welcomed.

games.q: your cousin admits he's not sure he believes the family's teachings anymore, and he's scared to say so at home. by the Kalama Sutta, what helps most?
o: tell him to keep quiet until the feeling passes.
say the doubt is fair, and he can test what helps or harms.
tell him to drop whatever he can't prove right now.
games.why: the Buddha called doubt fitting in an uncertain matter, then offered a way to check. honest and tested, not hidden and not walked away from.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one doubt you really have, in plain words, without softening it. Under it, write one way you could test it in your own life this month.
Then sit with the paper face down beside you, and let the doubt be there without arguing it away.

wordCard.voice: Doubt: one kind, vicikiccha, wavers and never tries. The other kind asks, and then goes and checks.

orig.note: Pali: doubt, wavering; listed among the hindrances that cloud the mind.

carryVoice: Doubt, honestly: the Buddha told the Kalamas their doubt was fitting, and then handed them a test. Sleep well.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta, also called Kesaputta Sutta)
Digha Nikaya 2 (Samaññaphala Sutta: the hindrances, doubt among them)
